A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReSo study. All 20 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, were readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, a training curve, and agent-selection analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds standard-benchmark evaluations, a single-agent control, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The stated DAG construction, UCB selection, CRM evaluation, and DADB updates remain unchanged. However, v3 Figure 2(c) depicts CRM evaluating outputs during testing, whereas v1 explicitly excludes this and v3 Section 3.4 still says testing requires no reward model. The intended inference procedure is therefore ambiguous.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluations on GSM8K, GPQA, HumanEval, and MMLU, extending coverage to programming and broader knowledge tasks. These replace the original MATH/SciBench comparison in Table 2. Math-MAS, SciBench-MAS, and the appendix evaluations of their constituent subproblems remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains its comparator set. The secondary standard-benchmark comparison changes from GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o, SEDM, and GPTSwarm to DyLAN, GDesigner, and GPTSwarm, alongside the benchmark replacement. SEDM is no longer evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 reports adding code-specialist agents beyond the existing 63 for HumanEval, introduces a single-agent control, and adds runtime as an evaluation measure. The decomposition ablation specifies GPT-4o instead of GPT-4, although identical plotted values do not establish rerunning. Existing synthetic-data splits, fine-tuning budgets, and numerical hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix J adds a control testing whether a fine-tuned decomposer suffices without multi-agent cooperation. Appendix C replaces the mathematics synthesis example with a scientific-task example showing explicit agent routing. The three existing component ablations and appendix agent-selection analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained plots and tables preserve the same point-estimate reporting, and the new tables do not introduce uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 is unchanged, including ReSo's hard-task accuracies of 33.7% and 32.3%. The original Table 2 results are replaced by new benchmark results: ReSo scores 95.70 on GSM8K, 55.80 on GPQA, 92.00 on HumanEval, and 88.70 on MMLU. Tables 3–4 add control and runtime outcomes; these are new comparisons rather than same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: The formal task and graph definitions, Equations 1–8, and Section 3.5's computational-complexity argument are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: v3's introduction explicitly acknowledges prior agent-selection and task-decomposition work and identifies their integrated formulation as the principal contribution. This refines the novelty framing while retaining the headline CRM, self-organizing MAS, automatic synthesis, and performance claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.4 substantially expands interpretations of agent scalability, training-data benefits, and domain applicability. New Appendices H–K discuss CRM versus PRM, limitations of single-model CoT, attribution of gains to cooperation rather than Qwen alone, and computational tradeoffs. The original limitations and reward-hacking discussion remain.

D1.justification: Appendix I newly clarifies that existing single-model prompts support CoT-style reasoning, and Appendix K reports 3 hours of training plus 1.1 hours of testing for ReSo. The repository link, prompt listings, and hyperparameters are retained. The detailed synthesis JSON example is replaced by an abbreviated example, reducing some reproducibility detail.

R1.justification: v3 adds explicit positioning of ReSo as an integration of prior mechanisms and discusses its relationship to PRM and CoT. Several references are removed, including the SEDM paper and Rewarding Progress. Most related-work content is retained; the author-year citation conversion is presentational.

P1.justification: The core method and data-synthesis prose remain largely verbatim. v3 revises the introduction and case study, reorganizes contributions and experimental discussion, moves reward-signal and token-efficiency discussion into appendices, and changes appendix organization, author text, and citation style.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is completely redesigned, the redundant main benchmark bar chart is removed, and the original synthesis listing and DAG display are replaced by a compact formatted case study. Table 2 receives different rows and columns, and Tables 3–4 are added. The training curve and several retained appendix displays are relocated.

improvement.justification: Broader benchmark coverage, the cooperation control, and runtime reporting add useful evidence. However, the new evaluations lack corresponding protocol detail, the original standalone benchmark comparison is removed, and redesigned Figure 2 introduces a contradiction with Section 3.4 about CRM use during testing. These benefits and reporting problems leave the net quality direction uncertain.
